concept.name: Synthetic short stock
concept.definition: A synthetic short stock position is a short call and a long put at the same strike and expiration on the same underlying; by put-call parity its payoff replicates being short the underlying, losing or gaining point-for-point as the stock rises or falls from the strike.
concept.intuition: You get the payoff of a short sale without borrowing shares: below the strike the put pays, above it the short call obliges you to sell — either way you are effectively short from the strike.
concept.mechanics: At expiration the combined value equals K - S_T (plus any net premium adjustment), matching a forward sale at K. The structure avoids stock-borrow costs and hard-to-borrow constraints, but the short call is naked with theoretically unlimited risk, and no borrow means no rebate considerations but also margin on the call.
concept.formula: Value at expiration = max(K - S_T, 0) - max(S_T - K, 0) = K - S_T; initial credit P - C approximates PV(K) - S_0 by put-call parity.
concept.failure_modes: The naked short call has unlimited loss in a rally or short squeeze — worse than a stock short in that it cannot be 'covered' by holding shares; assignment on the ITM short call (especially before ex-dividend dates) can force delivery and create borrow needs the structure was meant to avoid.
concept.misconceptions: Avoiding the borrow does not avoid short-seller economics: the options market prices in borrow difficulty through put-call parity (expensive puts / cheap calls), so hard-to-borrow names simply shift the cost into the option prices.
concept.example: With XYZ at $100, sell the $100 call for $4.50 and buy the $100 put for $4.00 (net credit $0.50). If XYZ finishes at $85, the position gains $15, replicating a short sale from $100; above $100 losses are unlimited.
